title: Tobin and Nessa's Ribbon Rescue
markdown:
In Whiskerwind the houses were painted like breakfast: strawberry jam, lemon drops, a rash of blueberry doors. Lampposts had little smiles built into them, and on bright mornings those smiles seemed to mean it. Tobin lived there, and he was the swiftest broomstick flyer in town. His fingers were quick as sparrows. His smile could chase a grumpy cloud until the cloud forgot what it had been sulking about. By his side, always, was Nessa. She was a cloud kitten: not whiskers-and-paws in the ordinary way, but a fluffy floaty creature made of the softest puff imaginable, white as a snowy day and light as a sigh. When she purred, it sounded like tiny faraway bells chiming a happy tune. Zip and zoom, said the wind in Tobin's hair. Chime and purr, said Nessa.

They were practising for the Great Sky-Ribbon Race, the most exciting event of the year. Racers zipped and zoomed through the blue. Brooms left glitter-trails that sparkled like fallen stars. High above, special weather ribbons were strung from the very top of the Whispering Bell Tower: a sunshine ribbon, a gentle-breeze ribbon, a refreshing-sprinkle ribbon, and a soft fluffy cloud ribbon. Sunshine, breeze, sprinkle, and cloud. When the race began, a gust-spell was meant to pull them into just the right order, for perfect racing weather, of course.

Tobin tried a daring loop-the-loop. His heart thrummed. Nessa purred on his shoulder, a contented chime. The town tilted and righted itself, jam-coloured roofs spinning like sweets in a jar.

Then — WHOOSH!

A funny mischievous gust, a gust that had clearly gone off on its own holiday, came swirling through Whiskerwind. It tugged and it pulled. It spun and it twirled with all its might. Before Tobin could shout whoa, the beautiful weather ribbons ripped from their hooks on the Bell Tower and went into a whirling snapping tangle that smelled of ozone and hurried dust.

"Oh, goodness gracious!" gasped Tobin. His sunshine smile went out like a lamp in a draught. The bright yellow sunshine ribbon was tangled with the watery sprinkle. The soft cloud ribbon was snagged all around the breezy blue one, lumpy as a grumpy balloon. "The town fair opens at noon! If those ribbons aren't right, we could have a sudden snow flurry during the cake-eating contest, or a scorching hot day when everyone wants to play tag!" He wrung his hands. A wobbly feeling started to bubble in his tummy, shaky and uncertain, as if the broom itself had turned to jelly.

Nessa nudged his cheek with her cloud-soft head. Her bell-purr was more of a worried rustle this time. "We must fix it, Tobin," she whispered, gentle as a summer breeze that still means business.

The Whispering Bell Tower was very old and very secret. Not just anyone could waltz in. Only the town's most skillful weather-weavers knew its hidden ways, and the only entrance was a tiny forgotten door, tucked away where no one usually looked.

"The Bell Tower!" Tobin said, eyes wide with a spark of hope. "That's where the ribbons are tied. We have to get inside and put them back."

And that very morning Tobin's aunt, who was the chief weather-weaver and wore spectacles on the very tip of her nose, had — quite by accident — left that tiny service door ajar. Just a little crack. A wonderfully lucky crack.

Tobin took a deep steadying breath. "Come on, Nessa!" Quick steps toward the grand imposing stone. Down below, the joyful sounds of the town fair were just beginning to drift up: a fiddle testing a string, a laugh, the clink of a plate being set for later pie.

They squeezed through the narrow gap. Inside was a vast shadowy space. The air smelled of old wood and a faint coppery tang. Dust motes danced in the few slivers of sunlight that managed to peek through the tall round windows far, far above. A low quiet hum filled the air, like a sleeping giant breathing. The chilly stone walls seemed to press in, smelling of old dust and forgotten secrets. Tobin held Nessa close. Her little cloud-paws dug ever so gently into his shoulder.

"It's so enormous in here," he breathed, and his voice came back to him, smaller. Distant peals of laughter and lively music from the fair made the worry feel a size larger. The ticking — somewhere in the gears — was the sound of the fair's opening, already under way.

They tiptoed deeper. The path was dim. Strange clanking whirring sounds echoed from the giant gears and levers that controlled all of Whiskerwind's weather. Tobin's heart beat like a runaway drum. He thought of the race, of how much he longed to win. A small selfish whisper said, What if we just leave it? Maybe someone else will fix it. Maybe it won't be that bad.

"Look!" Nessa pointed with a tiny soft cloud-paw toward a wobbly wooden ramp. It climbed toward a higher, seemingly quicker way. A super-fast shortcut. A way to fix things in a flash and maybe even get Tobin back to the fair for a little more practice. Zip and zoom. Very tempting.

Tobin paused. He pictured himself flying, wind in his hair, the crowd cheering. Then he pictured the tangled mess far above, still looking sad and wrong. What if that ramp was not safe? What if it led to a dead end, or a drop, or a gear that did not care about boys and cloud kittens?

"No, Nessa," he said, shaking his head. "It's too risky. We have to do it the proper way. The safe way." Right over want. He felt the choice settle, not as a speech, as a step.

They took the steady sensible path, winding up through the heart of the tower. Enormous gears turned slowly, making sleepy rumbling sounds. Huge coiled springs looked like slumbering metallic serpents. The air grew cooler. The tinkling of the weather ribbons became clearer and clearer, a wrong music, knots instead of notes. Sunshine, breeze, sprinkle, and cloud — all talking at once, all tangled.

And then they saw it. Right at the top, just beneath the great booming bell, hung the weather ribbons, a sorry snarl. The sunshine ribbon was draped over the sprinkle, making the sunshine look watery and weak. The cloud ribbon was wrapped around the breeze, causing it to puff in odd lumpy shapes.

"Oh, dearie me," Tobin whispered.

The mayor's voice began to boom from the town square, announcing the start of the fair. The ticking was louder than ever, a frantic heartbeat. Untangling each ribbon meant saying goodbye to any hope of finishing his race, and perhaps even missing the very beginning of the fair. He reached out. The sunshine ribbon felt warm and smooth, like a sun-baked pebble. The sprinkle ribbon was cool and damp, smelling faintly of morning dew. He worked slowly and precisely, nimble fingers untying knots with great care. A glitter of old race-dust shook free and hung in a sun-sliver. Nessa perched on a high wooden beam and watched with wide encouraging eyes. She let out a soft chime-purr that sounded like hope, a little bell saying go on, go on.

He placed the sunshine ribbon on its hook. Then the breeze ribbon, making sure it fluttered and danced freely, a blue tongue of wind. Next the sprinkle ribbon, which gave off a faint refreshing scent, as if a cloud had decided to be kind. And finally the soft fluffy cloud ribbon, which billowed gently like a sleepy sheep. As he hung the very last one, a perfect bright beam of sunshine broke through the tower window, followed by a gentle playful breeze that tickled Tobin's cheeks. Sunshine, breeze, sprinkle, and cloud — in order, at last, as if the sky had remembered its manners.

"We did it!" Tobin whispered. The smile that came back was not only excitement. It was accomplishment, warm and glowing. He had chosen the town over the race he loved, and the choice was done, not a lecture, a set of four hooks holding four honest weathers.

Down below the town fair burst into life. The sun shone with all its might. A gentle breeze rustled the colourful banners. The delightful scent of freshly baked apple pies drifted up even through the coppery tower air. The mayor, looking up at the perfectly arranged ribbons, beamed.

Tobin and Nessa slipped out, hearts as light as dandelion fluff, faces dusty and glad. They had not won the race. They watched the townsfolk enjoying the perfect weather — tag on cool grass, cakes without snow, banners that behaved — and Tobin knew, without anyone needing to tell him, that this was the better prize. The mayor, seeing them emerge, waved them over and personally gave them the very first, biggest slices of the prize-winning apple pie. Zip and zoom could wait. Chime and purr, said Nessa, tasting cinnamon. The lampposts kept smiling. The ribbons held. And Whiskerwind, jam-coloured and lemon-bright, had the noon it had been promised.
